newsitem.title: USA: St. Paul agency sends last word to bondholders.
newsitem.headline: St. Paul agency sends last word to bondholders.

text.p: In an unusual move, the St. Paul, Minn., Port Authority on Friday issued a final explanatory report on $245 million of revenue bonds headed towards default in the future.

Mike Strand, spokesman for the authority, said the report was unusual because the bonds in question are not subject to the Securities and Exchange Commission's secondary market reporting requirements.
"Unusual conditions call for unusual measures," Strand said, referring to the authority's five-year attempt to restructure its Resolution 876 Common Revenue Bond Fund bonds inorder to avoid default.
The latest restructuring attempt ended earlier this month when the authority announced it was unable to reach a consensus with a majority of bondholders and was in effect, giving up.
Strand said given the time and energy put into the restructuring, the authority decided to pull the story of the bond fund together.
The report lays out the history of the real estate projects funded by lease revenue bonds under the resolution and three failed attempts to restructure that debt.

The report also shows that reserve funds, currently used to subsidize negative cash flow for debt service on the bonds, will be depleted by 2003 or sooner if 13 of the 21 properties repossed by the authority are not sold. The depletion of sufficient reserves to pay all debt service payments will lead the authority to first pay current interest on the bonds on a pro rata basis. After that, the authority will use remaining funds to pay principal only on the bonds on a pro rata basis.
In 1996, the authority projected a $132.8 million shortfall between revenues and debt service needs from 1996 until the bonds' ultimate maturity in 2022, according to the report.
Strand said the authority will not be making any future projections on available funds to pay off the bonds.
"Whatever happens, happens and whatever (money) there is will be redistributed," he said.
However, the authority will be issuing annual audits of the fund, he added.
In the meantime, the port authority is current on debt service payments on the bonds, which the report said "appear to be actively traded in the marketplace."
Strand pointed out that some retail investors have been selling their bonds at a discount.

The report also addresses questions such as the possibility of a turnaround in the St. Paul real estate market to rescue the bonds. But Strand said real estate values would have to experience three-digit increases for that to happen.

The authority has issued nearly $429 million of industrial and commercial revenue bonds under Resolution 876 since 1974 to finance 139 real estate loans for a variety of properties, including hotels and office buildings. The report indicated that a depressed real estate market led to the repossession of 35 of the properties by the authority, although some of those properties were subsequently resold.
